To give without taking is not human. That would be God’s affair. And specifically the affair of a God who can create the world out of nothing.
And that is exactly what is missing.
Nobody can baptize this strange child, this capitalist who develops purchasing power.
“Fordism” is not really a name either.

Socialism, by contrast, as I said, still has a certain ring to it despite everything. And that gives it a historical legitimacy powerful enough to make 200 million Russians, practicing ascetic renunciation of their own consumption, “develop” more than 600 million Chinese, Indonesians, and other peoples!
I read the chapter “Plotnoi” in Mutius’s Katorgan and became suspicious because it smelled too much like Ernst Jünger’s Forest Passage.
How does one undermine today’s world domination?
The way early Christianity undermined the Roman Empire?
That would be the problem of asceticism.
Anyone practicing asceticism today is sabotaging the pure consumer society.

The Russians can justify being ascetics today only by claiming that they are organizing an even more comfortable consumer society for tomorrow. Otherwise they would be the saboteurs of the new Paradise.
The patriot, as such, is neither a producer nor a consumer. So what exactly does he want?
He must go on strike. But even the strike, if properly organized, can become an institution of the pure consumer society.
I do not know how Nicolaus ended up with a subject like this.
Bavarian Radio probably hung it around his neck.
I would rather give a lecture on the Bavarian Party and the electoral threshold.
“Those bells were never yours, and they are no longer mine.”
You must know them if you want to understand my life. They stand at the beginning of the German twentieth century.
At the time they were written, I was a naive thirteen-year-old country boy madly infatuated with a Jewish girl named Meta Gutmann.

I could never have guessed that a poet from the generation before mine, with deeper knowledge, was writing lines like these. And it would have done no good if someone had quoted them to me and explained them when I was thirteen.
Everything would have disappeared beneath my completely Catholic upbringing and my rebellion against it.
Yet I have never found them quoted, much less interpreted.
People passed over them then and continue to pass over them today. And how easily they can be extended:
Those were never your myths, and they are no longer mine.
Those were never your wines, and they are no longer mine.
Those were never your poets, and they are no longer mine.
Here, admittedly, the extension seems to fail. But this remains:
Those were never your saints, and I cannot part from them.
Peter Schneider’s book State of Exception and Norm: A Study of the Legal Theory of C. S. has finally appeared.
It is presumably intended to de-Schmittize German jurisprudence.
A Swiss man who went through none of it summons me, who went through all of it, before his tribunal.
A neutral man without a fate of his own passes judgment on my fate.

At bottom it is completely incompetent. But it is symptomatic and symbolic. And that is how I want to accept it, without irony or polemic, as one part of the general fate, like everything else: without submitting, but also without defending myself. It would be contrary to the style and the esprit de mon âge—the spirit of my age in life—to raise questions of jurisdiction, standing, or legal authority to bring the case.
Walter Warnach thinks, rightly, that Catholics are more restrained in their speech than Protestants.
Since Catholicism stopped being a religion of the people, with whom can a Catholic speak freely and without concern?
Priests cannot speak freely among themselves.
Laypeople cannot speak freely among themselves.
Priests cannot speak freely with laypeople.
Laypeople cannot speak freely with priests.
Secularized priests and secularized laypeople continue this habit for generations.
Polla ta deina—many are the terrible things.
Many terrible things I have seen.
Of many terrible things I have heard.
But the most terrible—but the most terrible—is and remains—nobody understands it;

nobody can grasp it: the most terrible thing is and remains the celibate bureaucracy that finds itself facing a reality—which it has itself helped create—in which Christianity is not even “Judaism for the people” anymore; and which now, in this admittedly precarious situation, looks around for new sources of strength—and of money.
This book by Peter Schneider has no form. It is a cancerous growth of extensive excerpts from a few of my writings, with my life’s work slobbered over by bland C. G. Jung ideas.
The book has no form because it has no fate. But not fate-less like Hölderlin’s sleeping infant. Fate-less like a Swiss man whose country has been neutral for more than a hundred years.
How was this author supposed to digest a life’s work such as mine? And how was he allowed to appear before the German public while suffering from such obvious digestive problems?

Meanwhile Hans Zehrer blows a tremendous trumpet blast into empty space by publishing an article on the permanent state of exception in Die Welt of 30 March 1957. It is a magnificent, though anonymous, German answer to the Swiss book’s complete lack of connection with reality. Zehrer dares to say openly that atomic power—which by its nature depends on secrecy—and democracy—which demands complete publicity—are incompatible.
Today, when a small sworn circle decides matters concerning the atom, we live under a permanent state of exception that more or less suspends democracy.
Faced with concrete realities like these, our Swiss ostrich prefers to stick his head into a bowl of whipped cream.

Behind my work on the state of exception lies the problem of the limits of what our modern, highly divided social machinery calls “law.” It is the problem of the limits of the courts and of judicial procedure.
The limit of what a modern legislator can turn into a statutory rule.
The limits of norms and normativity as such.
Naturally, asking about these limits brings one directly up against the territory of secrets and taboos.
As a young, inexperienced jurist, guided by no genuine teacher of constitutional or international law, I made a number of mistakes and violated more than one taboo.
That was serious and deserves correction. If Peter Schneider had asked and answered the question in that way, his book would have been magnificent, even if it had not been exhaustive.

Instead, as he calls it, he approaches the matter “anthropologically,” using a thin infusion of C. G. Jung’s categories, and asks about my personal secret—my Arcanum—on p. 96 of his book and elsewhere. And he ignores—with what right, exactly?—the passage in Ex Captivitate Salus, p. [75], where I formally deposited that Arcanum. He would have done better to consider my reference to the connection between dictatorship, sovereignty, and grace in the preface to Dictatorship, p. IX. And he should have remembered Rivarol’s warning not to betray the “perplexity of justice” and not to deal with problems “for which Themis has no scales.”
Peter Schneider’s book pushes me further into the problem of the judicial process itself:
Each of the three peoples that shaped European thought—the Greeks, the Romans, and the Jews—had one man who, for us Europeans, was their greatest.
Each of these three peoples killed its greatest man.
But only the people with the strongest sense of law and legal procedure—the Romans—did not kill their Julius Caesar judicially.

Queen Elizabeth of England sensed in 1585/86, through the instinct of royal blood, that it would have been less dangerous to the principle of monarchy to have Mary Stuart killed informally than to subject her to a formal trial before judges and an executioner appointed and authorized by Elizabeth herself.
She sensed the great precedent that would later lead to Cromwell’s trial and judicial killing of her successor Charles I in 1649.
And finally to the death blow against European monarchy: the judicial killing of Louis XVI by the Jacobins in 1793.
Compare J. E. Neale, Elizabeth and Her Parliaments 1584–1601, London, Jonathan Cape, 1957, pp. 140 ff.
The killing of Wallenstein in 1634, according to Pekař.
Under the impact of the judicial killing of Louis XVI, Kant wrote in his Doctrine of Right, Part II, General Remark, Meiner edition pp. 142 ff.:

“Even the murder of the monarch is not yet the worst thing—for one can still imagine that it was done out of fear—because it does not claim to be an act of punitive justice but an act of self-preservation.
It is the formal execution that fills a soul imbued with the rights of man with horror…”
The “complete overturning of all concepts of right”—Charles I, Louis XVI.
“That is the crimen mortale, inexpiabile—the mortal, unatonable crime—at bottom inexplicable because the criminal knowingly acts against the law,” and so on.
The reversal of the relationship between sovereign and people.
